entries: Borrowed from Middle Low German beschênigen (14th c.), extended form of beschênen, from be- + Proto-West Germanic *skainijan (“to make appear”). This latter verb is a causative of *skīnan, whence German scheinen (“to shine, appear”). It was borrowed along the Lower Rhine in the 15th century and fully established itself in High German during the 16th. Due to the merger of West Germanic ai and ī, it appears to be derived as be- + Schein + -ig + -en. In truth, the noun Schein is closely related, but does not underlie directly.

* Jacob Grimm and Václav Machek think it derives from Slavic (whence also Schmetten and English smetana). See смета́на (smetána) for more.

entries:
Via German Low German stūr from Middle Low German stūr, stūre, ultimately from the root of stehen (“to stand”).
The word is first attested in standard German in the 19th century, but speedily became part of the core vocabulary. Cognate with Dutch stoer (itself a form of dialectal origin), Swedish stursk and with Old High German stūr, stūri, stiuri (“strong, big, stately, proud”). Outside of Germanic, cognate with Sanskrit स्थूर (sthūra, “strong, large, thick”).
